findings.claim: when asked to evaluate, always give one positive and one negative impact — examiners are checking you can weigh both sides, not just list effects
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner behaviour. The Component 3 assessment rules supplied (specification pages 3, 21-27) say only that the paper uses structured data response questions, some requiring extended responses, and set AO weightings; they say nothing about what examiners are 'checking' in evaluate questions.
findings.correction: when asked to evaluate, give both a positive and a negative impact and reach an overall judgement, because an evaluation needs both sides weighed rather than a list of effects.

findings.claim: The area served by, or dependent on, a larger urban centre is called its _____. Options: catchment / hinterland / transect / sample (correct: hinterland)
findings.problem: The question has two defensible answers within this lesson: the glossary and the in-text definition of 'catchment' given here are 'The area served by, or dependent on, a larger urban centre for jobs, shopping or services' — word for word the stem of this question. A student choosing 'catchment' would be following the lesson's own definition and would be marked wrong.
findings.correction: Reword the stem so only one option fits: 'The rural area surrounding a town or city that depends on it for jobs and services is called its _____.' Options: catchment / hinterland / transect / sample (correct: hinterland) — and narrow the glossary definition of 'catchment' so it is not identical (see glossary finding).

findings.claim: catchment: The area served by, or dependent on, a larger urban centre for jobs, shopping or services.
findings.problem: Too narrow and duplicates the lesson's definition of 'hinterland'. The specification (Table B, Sphere of influence) uses 'catchment' more broadly — 'sphere of influence / catchment area' of urban areas, honeypot sites and landscape features, and also 'river catchment and its impact on potential flood risk' — a usage this definition excludes, even though the lesson itself refers to a river catchment.
findings.correction: catchment: The area from which a place, site or feature draws its users, or from which a river collects its water — used in the specification for both the catchment area of a service or honeypot site and a river catchment.

findings.claim: Two years before each exam series, your exam board names one methodological approach from Table A and one conceptual framework from Table B.
findings.problem: Slight imprecision against the specification, which states that teachers are notified 'at least two years in advance' (Section 2.3, Component 3) — the published sheet in fact lists approaches to 2030, well over two years ahead.
findings.correction: At least two years before each exam series, your exam board names one methodological approach from Table A and one conceptual framework from Table B.

findings.claim: Whether you write about a transect or a place enquiry, examiners expect the same evaluative language: comment on the accuracy of your measurements, the reliability of your sample size and repeat readings, and any possible bias
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about examiner behaviour. Neither the stated assessment rules nor the specification says what examiners 'expect'. The underlying content is sound — specification skill 1.6 requires learners to 'Identify the limitations of geographical evidence: accuracy, reliability and bias' — so the claim should be attributed to the specification, not to examiners.
findings.correction: Whether you write about a transect or a place enquiry, the specification requires the same evaluative language: comment on the accuracy of your measurements, the reliability of your sample size and repeat readings, and any possible bias — for instance a transect walked only in good weather, or two locations compared using different observers.

findings.claim: You decide the sampling interval and set up control points: fixed locations or repeated conditions that let you check whether an unusual reading is caused by the feature you are studying, or by something else, such as recent rain or an eroded footpath.
findings.problem: The specification's fieldwork skill 1.2 uses the term 'Establish control groups', not 'control points'. Inventing a near-miss technical term risks students using non-specification vocabulary.
findings.correction: You decide the sampling interval and establish control groups: comparison locations or repeated conditions that let you check whether an unusual reading is caused by the feature you are studying, or by something else, such as recent rain or an eroded footpath.

findings.claim: In the exam, Part A questions will ask about a transect enquiry and Part B questions will ask about a place enquiry — sometimes using an unfamiliar example, sometimes asking you to draw on the enquiry your class carried out.
findings.problem: The specification text states only that Part A assesses approaches to fieldwork methodology, representation and analysis and Part B assesses how fieldwork enquiry may be used to investigate conceptual frameworks, using 'structured data response questions, some of which will require extended responses'. It does not state that some questions use unfamiliar examples while others require candidates to write about their own fieldwork, so this detail about question format is not supported by the stated assessment rules.
findings.correction: In the exam, Part A questions are set on fieldwork methodology (transects for 2028) and Part B questions on the conceptual framework (place for 2028), using structured data response questions, some of which require extended responses.
